title: Sad. Then an oath by a Book full of reminding.
subtitle: Pausing before a surah about stubborn pride
then: The surah opens with the single letter Sad. Its meaning is known to Allah. Then comes an oath by the Quran, which Ibn Kathir explains as {idea}a reminder and a benefit for people in this life and the next{/idea}, and also a Book of high honor. Both meanings fit together.
now: You open the app on the bus, half reading, thumb ready to scroll. A single letter sits there that you cannot decode. {idea}That is the point: stop, and listen to what comes next.{/idea} A reminder only works on someone who slows down.
old: I already know what the Quran says, more or less.
new: It is a reminder, and a reminder needs me to pause and actually pay attention.
try: Before you read today, sit still for ten seconds and ask: what do I need reminding of?

title: The reminder was there. Pride stood in the way.
subtitle: Why a clear message still gets rejected
then: The Quran held a lesson for anyone willing to learn. The leaders of Makkah did not benefit, because they were in {trap}false pride and opposition{/trap}. Ibn Kathir says this means arrogance, tribal loyalty, and stubbornly going against the message.
now: Your sibling gives you advice that is exactly right. You know it is right. But it came from your younger sibling, in front of the family chat. {trap}So you argue the opposite.{/trap} The problem was never the advice.
old: If I reject something, it is because it was not convincing.
new: Sometimes I reject what is true only because accepting it would cost my pride.
try: Recall one piece of good advice you brushed off because of who said it. Take one step on it today.

title: They cried out when the door had already closed.
subtitle: Turning back while there is still time
then: Allah reminds Quraysh of how many nations before them were destroyed. When the punishment came, they called out. Muhammad bin Ka'b said {trap}they called for Tawhid and repentance when their lives were already over{/trap}. It was not the time for escape.
now: The car warning light has been on for weeks. You meant to book the garage. Then it breaks down on the motorway at night. {idea}The light was mercy. Ignoring it was the choice.{/idea} The door of turning back is open today.
old: I will sort out my relationship with Allah later, when life calms down.
new: There is a last moment for turning back, and I do not know when mine is.
try: Make one sincere moment of repentance today, before sleep, without waiting for a better time.

title: A warner from among them, so they called him a liar.
subtitle: When the messenger is too familiar to hear

row.title: he is just one of us

then: The idolaters of Makkah were amazed that {idea}a human being like themselves{/idea} came to them as a warner. Instead of weighing the message, the disbelievers gave it a label: {trap}a sorcerer, a liar{/trap}.
now: A colleague you have worked beside for years suggests a better way to run the team. Your first thought is not whether it works. It is: who is he to tell us. {trap}A label is faster than thinking.{/trap}
old: Someone ordinary like me cannot be bringing me something important.
new: Truth often arrives through someone familiar, so I judge the message, not the messenger.
try: Next time someone close tells you something hard, reply with a question instead of a label.

title: One God sounded strange to people raised on many.
subtitle: The shock of a single word: La ilaha illallah

row.title: One God
sub: strange only to a full heart

then: When Abu Talib was ill, the chiefs of Quraysh complained to him. The Prophet ﷺ said he wanted from them only {idea}one word{/idea}. They said they would give ten. When he said La ilaha illallah, they stood up in agitation saying {trap}has he made the gods into One God?{/trap}
now: You grew up with a way of doing things at home: a habit, a belief, a family rule. Someone points out it does not hold up. It feels like an attack, not because it is wrong, but because {trap}your heart is full of it.{/trap}
old: What I grew up with feels right, so anything else must be odd.
new: Familiar is not the same as true. A strange idea can be the clearest one.
try: Pick one inherited habit and ask honestly: do I do this for Allah, or only because we always have?

title: The chiefs walked out telling everyone: hold on to your gods.
subtitle: Patience used in the wrong direction
then: The leaders went out urging people to {trap}persist and stay constant to their gods{/trap}. They said this call was something designed. Ibn Jarir explains they claimed the Prophet ﷺ only wanted to gain power and followers through it.
now: Someone in the office proposes an honest change. The people who benefit from the old way start a side chat: he just wants a promotion. {trap}Assume a bad motive, and you never have to answer the point.{/trap}
old: If someone pushes for change, they must want something for themselves.
new: Accusing someone's motive is often a way to avoid facing what they said.
try: When you catch yourself guessing someone's hidden motive, respond to their actual words instead.

title: We never heard this before, so it must be made up.
subtitle: Using unfamiliarity as proof of falsehood
then: The chiefs said they had not heard of this Tawhid in {trap}the religion of these later days{/trap}. Ibn Abbas reported they meant Christianity: if this were true, the Christians would have told them. So they called it an invention.
now: Someone shares a reminder in the group chat that you have never come across. Your reply is ready before you read it: never heard of that. {idea}Never hearing something is a fact about you, not about it.{/idea}
old: If I have not heard of it, it is probably not real.
new: What I have not heard yet tells me where my knowledge ends, nothing more.
try: Look up one thing today you dismissed only because it was new to you.

title: Why him and not us? The question behind the doubt.
subtitle: Envy dressed up as skepticism

row.title: we decide who deserves
sub: the great men of the towns

then: Quraysh found it unlikely that {trap}he alone, out of all of them{/trap}, received the Reminder. Ibn Kathir links it to their wish that it had come to a great man of the two towns. Allah answers: they are in doubt, because they have not yet tasted the punishment.
now: A friend gets the opportunity you wanted. Your first comment is a doubt: are we sure it is real? Underneath is a simpler feeling. {trap}Why them and not me?{/trap} {idea}Gifts are not handed out by your vote.{/idea}
old: If someone else is chosen over me, something must be off.
new: Allah gives what He wills to whom He wills. My doubt may only be envy.
try: Congratulate one person today on something you secretly wished was yours.

title: Do they hold the keys to your Lord's mercy?
subtitle: The Mighty, the Bestower gives as He wills

row.title: the chiefs
sub: not even a speck of dust

then: Allah challenges them: do they own {reward}the treasures of the mercy of your Lord{/reward}? Ibn Kathir says His servants have no control over His dominion, not even the thin skin on a date stone. He is Almighty, and He gives whatever He wills.
now: You feel you know who deserves a second chance and who does not. The relative who messed up. The colleague who failed. {reward}Mercy is not your storeroom.{/reward} Neither is it locked to you when you are the one who failed.
old: I can tell who deserves Allah's mercy and who is beyond it.
new: The treasures of mercy belong to Allah alone, for others and for me.
try: Make a short dua today for someone you had quietly written off.

title: If the heavens are theirs, let them climb up and run them.
subtitle: A challenge that exposes empty authority
then: Ibn Kathir explains that Allah is the One in control of His creation, who gives and honors whom He wills. So He asks the deniers: is {idea}the dominion of the heavens and the earth{/idea} theirs? If so, {trap}let them ascend by any means{/trap}.
now: You plan the whole year on a spreadsheet: the job, the move, the wedding date. Then one phone call changes everything. {idea}You manage a few things. You own none of them.{/idea}
old: I am in charge of how my life turns out.
new: I can plan and work, but the control of everything belongs to Allah.
try: Add In sha Allah to one plan you mention today, and mean it.

title: Just one more army that will be defeated.
subtitle: The loud opposition is smaller than it looks

picture.label: How it looked vs. what it was

then: In Makkah the Prophet ﷺ and the believers were few and the chiefs were powerful. Allah describes those chiefs as {trap}a defeated host{/trap}, like the Confederates of old times. {idea}Their strength was temporary.{/idea}
now: You are the only one in the office who will not join the shady side deal. Everyone else seems to be on the other side. {idea}A crowd is not the same as strength.{/idea} Stay with what is right.
old: When everyone is against me, I must be losing.
new: Numbers and noise against the truth do not decide the ending.
try: Hold to one right choice today that you were tempted to drop because you were outnumbered.

title: Nuh's people, Ad, and Pharaoh of the stakes denied too.
subtitle: Others had more power and still fell
then: Allah lists nations who denied before Quraysh: the people of Nuh, Ad, and Pharaoh. Ibn Kathir says {trap}they were greater and stronger, with more wealth and children{/trap}, yet that did not protect them when the command of Allah came.
now: The big company everyone thought would last forever closes in a year. The famous name you thought untouchable falls. {idea}Strength is borrowed.{/idea} What lasts is how you answered the truth when it came to you.
old: If I am strong and secure enough, I am safe.
new: Even the strongest were not protected by strength. Only by their response to truth.
try: Write one thing you lean on for security, and next to it, one thing you can do for Allah today.

title: Thamud, Lut's people, the Thicket dwellers: those were the Confederates.
subtitle: A long line of people who chose the same way
then: The list continues with Thamud, the people of Lut, and the Dwellers of the Thicket. Allah calls them {trap}the Confederates{/trap}. Ibn Kathir notes their stories are told in detail in many places in the Quran. Here they are gathered into one line.
now: Everyone at school cheats on the online quiz. Everyone at work rounds up the hours. {trap}Being one of many does not change what the act is.{/trap} The crowd does not stand with you when you answer for it.
old: If many people do it, it cannot be that bad.
new: A wrong shared by many is still a wrong, and each person answers alone.
try: Notice one thing you do only because everyone around you does it. Skip it once.

title: Every one of them denied the messengers, so the penalty was just.
subtitle: The common thread behind every fallen nation
then: Ibn Kathir says {trap}the reason for their destruction was their disbelief in the Messengers{/trap}, so those being addressed should beware. Ibn Kathir also mentions this verse as one explanation for the oath at the start of the surah.
now: When things go wrong, you blame timing, the economy, the boss. Rarely do you ask about the warning you ignored. {idea}Honest reflection starts with your own choices.{/idea}
old: What happens to people is mostly circumstance.
new: Allah is never unjust. Consequences follow choices, so I look at mine first.
try: Think of one recent setback and ask what part your own choice played. No blame, just honesty.

title: They wait for only one blast, and it will not pause.
subtitle: The Hour arrives suddenly, without delay
then: Ibn Kathir explains this is {trap}the blast on the Trumpet{/trap}, when Israfil is commanded to sound it. Zayd bin Aslam said none can avert it. The Hour comes suddenly, while people do not perceive it, and some of its signs have already come.
now: You keep a list of things to fix: call your mother, return what you borrowed, pray on time. All of it is set for someday. {idea}Someday is not promised.{/idea} The good news is that today is still here.
old: There will be a clear signal before the end, and I will get ready then.
new: It comes without pause, so the time to be ready is now, with hope.
try: Do one thing from your someday list today. Just one.

title: Bring it on now, they said, mocking the Day of Account.
subtitle: Asking for consequences as a joke
then: The idolaters asked Allah to {trap}hasten their share before the Day of Reckoning{/trap}. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and others said they were asking for the punishment to come early. Ibn Jarir said they asked for whatever they deserved, good or bad, right now. Ibn Kathir says they said it in mockery.
now: Someone reminds you about the Day of Account and you laugh it off: if it is real, let it come. {trap}A joke can be a way of not thinking.{/trap} {idea}The delay is not proof it is false. It is time given to you.{/idea}
old: If consequences were real, they would have come already.
new: The delay is mercy and time, not evidence that nothing is coming.
try: Notice one serious thing you usually joke about. Sit with it quietly for a minute instead.

title: Be patient with their words, and remember Dawud, who kept returning.
subtitle: Strength that turns back to Allah again and again
then: The Prophet ﷺ is told to be patient and to remember Dawud. Ibn Kathir explains his strength as {idea}strength in knowledge, action and obedience{/idea}. The Prophet ﷺ said the most beloved prayer and fasting to Allah were those of Dawud, and that {reward}he always turned to Allah{/reward}.
now: Your manager's comment stings all afternoon. You could replay it on the drive home, or you could do what Dawud did: {idea}turn back to Allah, again{/idea}. Not once. Every time.
old: Being strong means not needing anyone.
new: Real strength keeps turning back to Allah, in every matter, again and again.
try: The next time someone's words hurt today, pause and say Astaghfirullah before you reply.

title: The mountains praised Allah with him, morning and evening.
subtitle: When your remembrance joins all of creation
then: Allah made {idea}the mountains glorify His praise with Dawud{/idea} at sunrise and at the end of the day. Ibn Kathir says the lofty mountains would echo his glorification. Ibn Abbas understood Salat Ad-Duha from the words ishraq, the time after sunrise.
now: Early morning, before the house wakes. You say SubhanAllah by the kitchen window and it feels small. {idea}It is not small.{/idea} The hills on the horizon are saying it too.
old: My little dhikr in the morning hardly counts for anything.
new: When I glorify Allah, I join something that mountains are part of.
try: Tomorrow after sunrise, say SubhanAllah ten times while looking at something in nature.

title: Even the birds gathered and joined his praise.
subtitle: A sincere voice draws others in
then: Ibn Kathir says if a bird flew by Dawud and heard him reciting the Zabur, {idea}it would not go away{/idea}. It stayed hovering in the air, glorifying Allah with him. All of them followed him in praise.
now: Your child hears you reciting softly after Fajr and comes to sit beside you without being asked. {reward}No lecture did that.{/reward} Sincere worship has its own pull.
old: To bring others to good, I have to push and convince them.
new: Sincere worship draws others in more than any argument can.
try: Recite a short surah aloud at home today where your family can hear, gently.

title: A strong kingdom, wisdom, and clear judgement in speech.
subtitle: The gifts that made Dawud a just ruler
then: Allah made Dawud's kingdom strong. Mujahid said he was the most powerful of the people of the world. He was also given {idea}wisdom and sound judgement{/idea}, which Mujahid explained as soundness in speech and in deciding cases. Ibn Kathir says this became a basis of judging in this Ummah.
now: You are the oldest sibling, and your word settles arguments at home. Or you lead a small team. {idea}Authority is a gift that needs wisdom{/idea}, and the wisdom to speak clearly and fairly.
old: Having authority means my opinion wins.
new: Any authority I have is a gift from Allah that comes with a duty to judge fairly.
try: In one disagreement today, hear both sides fully before you decide anything.

title: Two disputants climbed the wall into his private chamber.
subtitle: A test that came without warning
then: Ibn Kathir says many stories told about this passage come from {trap}Isra'iliyat narrations{/trap}, with nothing authentic from the Prophet ﷺ. So {idea}it is better to speak briefly and leave its knowledge to Allah{/idea}. Dawud was in his mihrab, the noblest part of his house, where no one was to enter that day.
now: A forwarded message tells a dramatic story about a prophet, full of details you have never seen. {idea}The Quran's own words are enough.{/idea} You do not need to fill the gaps with rumours.
old: The more detail a story has, the more I understand it.
new: When the source is silent, I stay with what is true and leave the rest to Allah.
try: Before forwarding a religious story today, check where it comes from. If unsure, do not send it.

title: Do not fear: judge between us with truth.
subtitle: A frightened judge still asked to be fair
then: Dawud {trap}was terrified of them{/trap} because they came in where no one was supposed to enter. They told him not to fear. They were two litigants, one had wronged the other, and they asked him to {idea}judge with truth and not be unjust{/idea}.
now: Your phone rings late and it is two cousins, both shouting, both wanting you on their side. Your heart is racing. {idea}Breathe, then be fair.{/idea} Fear and anger make poor judges.
old: When I am caught off guard, I cannot be expected to be fair.
new: Even when startled, I can settle myself and give each side the truth.
try: When someone brings you a complaint today, ask the other side before you take a position.

title: Ninety-nine ewes, and he still wanted my one.
subtitle: When having more makes someone want everything
then: One of the two said his brother had {reward}ninety-nine ewes{/reward} while he had one. The brother said hand it over, and {trap}overpowered him in speech{/trap}, meaning he defeated him in argument.
now: The big supplier squeezes the small shop owner on price because they can. The sibling with the bigger house still wants the inheritance split their way. {trap}Winning the argument is not the same as being in the right.{/trap}
old: If I can argue it well, it must be fair.
new: Being better at talking does not make taking from someone right.
try: Think of one place you hold more power than someone. Ask if you are taking more than your share.

title: He judged the case, then realized he was the one tested.
subtitle: Dawud fell in prostration and turned back
then: Dawud said the brother had wronged him, and that many partners oppress one another, {idea}except those who believe and do good, and they are few{/idea}. Then he understood Allah had tested him, and {reward}fell prostrate in repentance{/reward}. The Prophet ﷺ prostrated at this verse and said Dawud did it in repentance, and we do it in thanks.
now: You give your friend advice about being fair at work, and on the drive home you realize it applies to you. {reward}That moment is a gift.{/reward} Do not argue with it. Turn back.
old: When I see a fault, it is usually in someone else.
new: Sometimes the case I am judging is a mirror, and the right response is sajdah.
try: Make one sajdah today just to ask forgiveness for something you saw in yourself.

title: So We forgave him, and gave him nearness and a good return.
subtitle: Repentance that ends in closeness
then: Allah forgave him. Ibn Kathir says on the Day of Resurrection he will have {reward}nearness to Allah and the lofty levels of Paradise{/reward}, because of his repentance and his justice. He cites the hadith that those who are just with their families and those in their care will be on minbars of light.
now: You made a mistake you are ashamed of, and you think it has cancelled you. {reward}Repentance did not lower Dawud. It raised him.{/reward} The way back is also a way up.
old: After a serious mistake, I will always be less in Allah's sight.
new: Sincere repentance can bring me nearer to Allah than I was before.
try: Be fair to one person in your family or care today in a small, specific way.

title: Judge with truth and do not follow your desire.
subtitle: Advice to anyone given authority
then: Ibn Kathir calls this {idea}advice to rulers and leaders{/idea}. A scholar once reminded a Khalifah: are you dearer to Allah than Dawud? Allah gave Dawud prophethood and rule, and still warned him {trap}not to follow desire{/trap}. As-Suddi said the punishment comes for what they neglected to do for the Day of Reckoning.
now: You are the parent deciding who gets the car, the manager writing reviews, the class rep. You like one person more. {trap}Desire whispers the answer before the facts arrive.{/trap} Remember who will review your decision.
old: My judgement is fair because I am a fair person.
new: Anyone can be pulled by desire, even a prophet was warned, so I check myself.
try: Before one decision today, ask: would I decide the same if I disliked this person?

title: None of this was created without purpose.
subtitle: The heavens and earth point to a return
then: Ibn Kathir says Allah {idea}did not create the creatures in vain{/idea}. He created them to worship Him, then He will gather them. The idea that nothing comes after this world is {trap}the assumption of those who disbelieve{/trap}.
now: A long week of deadlines, laundry, and traffic. At night you wonder if any of it means anything. {idea}It does.{/idea} Every ordinary day sits inside a purpose bigger than the to-do list.
old: Most of my days are just routine, with no real point.
new: Nothing was created aimlessly, including my ordinary days.
try: Tonight, name one routine task and make an intention to do it for Allah tomorrow.

title: Would Allah treat the doers of good like the corrupters?
subtitle: Justice needs another world
then: Ibn Kathir says we see {trap}evildoers prospering until they die{/trap}, and oppressed believers dying in grief. Allah does not do a speck of injustice, so {idea}there must be a time when the rights of the oppressed are restored{/idea}. If not here, then in another realm.
now: The colleague who cut corners got the promotion. The honest one was let go. You start to think honesty is for fools. {idea}The account is not closed yet.{/idea} Keep doing good.
old: If cheaters win and the honest lose, being good does not pay.
new: Allah will not treat the good and the corrupt the same. The final account is still ahead.
try: Do one honest thing today that costs you a little, trusting the account is with Allah.

title: A blessed Book, sent down to be pondered.
subtitle: Reading to reflect, not just to finish
then: After showing that creation has a purpose, Allah describes the Quran as {reward}a Book full of blessings{/reward}, sent down so that people {idea}ponder its verses{/idea} and those with understanding remember. Ibn Kathir says it teaches sound aims through rational thinking.
now: Ramadan target: finish the whole Quran. You race through pages on your lunch break, barely tasting a word. {idea}One verse understood can do more than ten pages skimmed.{/idea}
old: Reading more pages is what counts.
new: The Book was sent to be pondered, so one verse I reflect on is a real step.
try: Pick one verse today. Read its meaning slowly three times and ask what it says to you.

title: Dawud was given Sulayman: an excellent servant, always turning back.
subtitle: A son praised for repentance, not his crown
then: Allah gave Sulayman to Dawud as a prophet, who {reward}inherited prophethood from him{/reward}. Ibn Kathir says the praise how excellent a servant is because Sulayman was very obedient, worshipped much, and {idea}always turned to Allah in repentance{/idea}.
now: Your parents bragged about your job title at the family dinner. {idea}Allah's praise for a king was about something else: that he kept coming back to Him.{/idea} That is the title worth having.
old: What makes someone excellent is what they achieve.
new: Allah calls a servant excellent for turning back to Him, whatever else they have.
try: Before bed, take one minute to turn back to Allah about something from today.

title: In the afternoon, his finest horses were paraded before him.
subtitle: Good things that fill the eye
then: Sulayman, as king, was shown {reward}well trained horses of the highest breed{/reward} in the afternoon. Mujahid said they stood on three legs and raised the fourth, and were swift. Ibn Kathir also mentions Aishah's toy horse with wings, which made the Prophet ﷺ smile broadly.
now: The new car in the driveway. The renovated kitchen. The laptop you saved for all year. {reward}Nice things are not the enemy.{/reward} But notice how long you stand there looking.
old: Loving good things is either totally fine or totally wrong.
new: Good things are a gift, and also a test of where my attention goes.
try: Thank Allah out loud for one nice thing you own, then put it down and move on.

title: Loving the good made him miss remembering his Lord.
subtitle: Distraction until the sun had set

row.title: own it
sub: I preferred the good over Him

then: More than one scholar said Sulayman was {trap}so busy looking at the horses that he missed Asr{/trap}. It was not deliberate but forgetfulness, like the day of Khandaq when the Prophet ﷺ prayed Asr after sunset. What stands out is that {idea}Sulayman named it plainly{/idea}.
now: You open your phone for one video before Maghrib. You look up and the adhan has long passed. {idea}Say it honestly: I let a good thing pull me away.{/idea} That honesty is the first step back.
old: Missing prayer for something harmless is not a big deal.
new: Even good things can push Allah aside, and I should notice when they do.
try: Set a reminder five minutes before your next prayer and put the phone face down when it rings.

title: Bring them back, he said, and dealt with what distracted him.
subtitle: Two scholarly readings of what he did

row.title: Al-Hasan, Qatadah
sub: he gave them up for Allah

row.title: pure loss
sub: I lose what I let go

then: Scholars differed. Al-Hasan and Qatadah said he gave the horses up, angry for the sake of Allah. Ibn Abbas said {idea}he patted their heads and legs out of love{/idea}, which Ibn Jarir preferred. Ibn Kathir notes that Allah then gave him {reward}the wind, faster and better than horses{/reward}, and cites the hadith: you do not give up anything for Allah but He gives you something better.
now: The game that eats your evenings. The app that keeps you up past midnight. You delete it and feel a small loss. {reward}What Allah gives back is usually better than what you let go.{/reward}
old: If I give something up for Allah, I just lose it.
new: Whatever I leave for Allah's sake, He replaces with something better.
try: Give up one small distraction for today only, for Allah's sake, and see what fills the space.

title: We tested Sulayman, then he turned back.
subtitle: Even a prophet-king was tested
then: Allah says He {trap}tested Sulayman{/trap} and placed a body on his throne. Ibn Kathir does not dwell on details. He says that {reward}after this test, he turned back to Allah{/reward} and asked forgiveness. The heading he gives is how Allah tested Sulayman, then made things easy for him.
now: Everything was going well: the job, the family, the plans. Then something knocks you sideways. {idea}A test is not a sign Allah has left you.{/idea} It is an invitation to come back.
old: If I am being tested, I must have lost Allah's favor.
new: Tests come even to the best of people, and the answer is to turn back to Him.
try: Name one hard thing you are going through and make a short dua about it tonight.

title: Forgive me first, then give me a kingdom like no other.
subtitle: A dua that starts with forgiveness
then: Sulayman asked, {idea}My Lord, forgive me{/idea}, then for a kingdom no one after him would have. The Prophet ﷺ once overpowered a jinn who tried to disturb his prayer and wanted to tie him to a pillar of the masjid, then {reward}remembered the dua of his brother Sulayman{/reward} and let him go.
now: You hold back in dua because your request feels too big: the house, the cure, the job abroad. {reward}Sulayman asked for something unique, and called Allah the Bestower.{/reward} Begin with forgiveness, then ask freely.
old: I should only ask Allah for small, reasonable things.
new: I start by asking forgiveness, then I ask the Bestower boldly.
try: Make one dua today that begins with Astaghfirullah and then asks for something big.

title: The wind was made to run gently at his command.
subtitle: What he let go was replaced with better
then: Al-Hasan Al-Basri said that when Sulayman gave up the horses for the sake of Allah, {reward}Allah compensated him with something better and swifter{/reward}: the wind. Its morning covered a month's journey and its evening a month's journey, blowing gently {idea}wherever in the world he wanted{/idea}.
now: You turned down the overtime that cut into Friday prayer. You worried about the money. Months later, a better door opens. {reward}It rarely looks like a straight swap.{/reward} It is usually better.
old: What I give up for Allah, I expect back in the same form.
new: Allah's replacement can come in a form I never imagined, and better.
try: Recall one thing you once gave up for Allah, and look for what came after it. Say Alhamdulillah.

title: Builders and divers among the jinn worked for him.
subtitle: Power over what others could not reach
then: Ibn Kathir says some jinn {idea}built high rooms, images, basins like reservoirs and fixed cauldrons{/idea}, tasks humans could not do. Others {reward}dived into the sea for pearls and jewels{/reward}. All of it was subjected to Sulayman by Allah.
now: Your team delivers the project. The car starts, the bank transfer goes through, the doctor finds the problem. {idea}So much works for you that you did not make.{/idea} Every helper is a gift placed in your path.
old: What I have achieved is down to my own effort and ability.
new: Everything that serves me was made to serve me by Allah.
try: Thank one person today who makes your work or life easier, and thank Allah for them.

title: And others bound together in chains.
subtitle: Rebellion was restrained, not rewarded
then: Ibn Kathir says those {trap}bound in fetters{/trap} were the ones who had rebelled and refused to work, or whose work was bad and who were wrongdoers. Sulayman's kingdom held power, and {idea}it also held wrongdoing in check{/idea}.
now: You have a temper, a habit, a craving that sometimes runs wild. {idea}Some things in you need to be tied down, not fed.{/idea} Strength includes restraining what does harm.
old: Everything I feel deserves to be let out.
new: Part of strength is restraining what in me does harm.
try: Pick one harmful habit and put one small barrier in its way today.

title: This is Our gift: give or hold back, no account asked.
subtitle: A freedom given, and a choice the Prophet ﷺ made
then: Allah told Sulayman his kingship was {reward}Our gift{/reward}, to give or withhold without being brought to account. Ibn Kathir notes the Prophet ﷺ was given the choice between being a king-prophet or a servant-messenger. He consulted Jibril, who said {idea}be humble{/idea}, so he chose to be a servant.
now: You get to choose: the bigger title with more control, or the quieter role where you serve. {idea}The Prophet ﷺ chose service.{/idea} Both can be good. Humility weighs more with Allah.
old: More control and status is always the better choice.
new: Everything I have is Allah's gift, and humble service is the higher path.
try: Do one quiet act of service today that no one will thank you for.

title: And for him: nearness to Us and a good return.
subtitle: Worldly power did not cost him the Hereafter
then: After all that Allah gave Sulayman in this world, He says Sulayman {reward}will have a great share with Him{/reward} on the Day of Resurrection. Ibn Kathir says this refers to {idea}this world and the Hereafter{/idea}. The same words were said of Dawud.
now: You worry that doing well, the raise, the business, the comfortable house, will pull you from Allah. {idea}It does not have to.{/idea} Sulayman had more than anyone and kept turning back.
old: Success in the world and closeness to Allah cannot go together.
new: With gratitude and repentance, what Allah gives me here need not cost me there.
try: Give a little from your next payment to someone in need, as thanks for what you have.

title: After years of loss, Ayyub called out to his Lord.
subtitle: Naming the pain to the One who can lift it
then: Ibn Kathir says Ayyub was tested in his body, wealth and children until {trap}no part of his body was healthy except his heart{/trap}. Relatives and strangers shunned him, except his wife, who worked for others to feed him. When the decreed time ended, he called on Allah. It was said distress meant his body and torment meant losing his wealth and children.
now: Months of hospital corridors, test results, missed work. People stopped asking. {idea}Ayyub's patience did not mean silence. It meant telling Allah.{/idea} You are allowed to say: it hurts, and You are the Most Merciful.
old: Being patient means never saying how much it hurts.
new: Patience can include crying out to Allah about my pain.
try: Tell Allah plainly, in your own words, one thing that is hurting you right now.

title: Strike the ground with your foot: cool water to wash and drink.
subtitle: Relief came from right under his feet
then: Allah told Ayyub to strike the ground with his foot. A spring flowed, he washed in it, and {reward}the pain in his body disappeared{/reward}. He struck again, drank from a second spring, and became healthy inside and out. In a narration, his wife {idea}did not recognise him at first{/idea}, he looked so well.
now: You have been searching for the answer everywhere: specialists, forums, late night searches. {reward}Sometimes the way out is closer than you think{/reward}, and comes with one small step that Allah blesses.
old: My relief must come from somewhere far and complicated.
new: When Allah wills relief, a small step can open it right where I stand.
try: Take one small step today toward something you have been stuck on, and say Bismillah first.

title: His family given back, and as many again, as mercy.
subtitle: Patience that ends in more than was lost
then: Al-Hasan and Qatadah said Allah {reward}brought his family back and added others like them{/reward}. Ibn Kathir says this mercy was in return for his patience, humility and constant turning to Allah. It is a reminder for those who understand that {idea}the consequence of patience is a way out{/idea}.
now: The years of waiting: for a child, a job, a healing. You wonder if patience is just a nice word for being stuck. {idea}Ayyub's story says it leads somewhere.{/idea}
old: Patience just means putting up with things that will never change.
new: Patience with turning to Allah ends in mercy and a way out.
try: Write down one hard season you already came through. Read it next time you feel stuck.

title: A way out of a hasty oath, and praise for his patience.
subtitle: Allah did not let her kindness be repaid with harm

picture.label: The problem and the way out

then: Ayyub had been upset with his wife and swore an oath in anger. Ibn Kathir asks how {reward}her service, mercy and kindness{/reward} could be repaid with harm. So Allah showed him a gentle way to keep his word without hurting her. Then Allah praised him: {idea}We found him patient, an excellent servant{/idea}.
now: Tired and angry, you said something to your spouse or child that you would never really do. {idea}Do not let a word spoken in anger outrank years of kindness.{/idea} Look for the way out that honors them.
old: Once I have said it, I have to follow through, even if it causes harm.
new: Allah opens a way out for those who fear Him, and kindness should be honored, not punished.
try: Apologise today for one thing you said in anger to someone who has been kind to you.

title: Ibrahim, Ishaq and Yaqub: people of strength and vision.
subtitle: Strong hands in worship, clear eyes in faith

key.label: What a full faith looks like

then: Allah tells the Prophet ﷺ to remember these servants, described as having {idea}hands and vision{/idea}. Ibn Kathir explains it as righteous deeds, beneficial knowledge, strength in worship and insight. Ibn Abbas said great strength in worship and understanding of the religion.
now: You know a lot of facts about Islam from videos. Or you pray a lot but rarely learn why. {idea}These prophets had both: strong in doing, clear in seeing.{/idea}
old: Either I study religion or I practice it.
new: The best of Allah's servants joined strong worship with deep understanding.
try: Learn the meaning of one thing you say in prayer, and pay attention to it next time.

title: Chosen for one quality: remembering the final Home.
subtitle: What set the prophets apart
then: Mujahid said Allah made them {idea}strive for the Hereafter{/idea}, with nothing else for them besides that. Malik bin Dinar said {trap}Allah removed the love of this world from their hearts{/trap}. Qatadah said they used to remind people about the final Home and strive for it.
now: Your phone is full of plans: the holiday, the next car, the house deposit. None of them are wrong. {idea}But which home are you saving for most?{/idea}
old: My future means my plans for the next few years.
new: The people Allah chose kept the final Home at the front of their minds.
try: Add one thing to your plans this week that only matters for the Hereafter.

title: With Us, they are among the chosen and the best.
subtitle: Whose opinion of you matters most
then: Allah says these servants are, {reward}with Us, among the chosen and the best{/reward}. Ibn Kathir explains they were elected and chosen. This was said while the Prophet ﷺ himself was being mocked in Makkah, a reminder that {idea}standing with Allah is what counts{/idea}.
now: You were passed over at work, or left out of the family plans, or ignored online. {idea}People's ranking changes every week.{/idea} The words with Us are what lasts.
old: How others see me shows what I am worth.
new: What matters is how I stand with Allah, not how I rank with people.
try: Do one good deed today that only Allah will see.

title: Remember Ismail, Al-Yasa and Dhul-Kifl: all among the best.
subtitle: Some names are short in the Quran but great with Allah
then: Allah adds three more names and says {reward}all are among the best{/reward}. Ibn Kathir says their stories and qualities were discussed in Surah Al-Anbiya. Here they are simply remembered together with honor.
now: Nobody will write a long post about you. Maybe a few lines at your funeral. {reward}A single line of praise from Allah is worth more than any biography.{/reward}
old: If no one tells my story, my life did not matter much.
new: A short mention with Allah among the best is the greatest honor.
try: Quietly do one good thing today that no one will ever post or mention.

title: This is a reminder, and the righteous have a good return.
subtitle: After the prophets' stories, the destination
then: After the prophets, Allah says {idea}this is a reminder{/idea}. As-Suddi said it means the Quran. Then He says the righteous will have {reward}a good final return{/reward}, which Ibn Kathir explains as their ultimate destination in the Hereafter.
now: You finished another story of a prophet and closed the app. {idea}It was not just a story. It was a reminder of where your road goes.{/idea} A good end is promised to those who guard themselves.
old: The stories of the prophets are about them, long ago.
new: They are reminders for me, pointing to a good return if I hold to taqwa.
try: Pick one quality from a prophet in this surah and practise it once today.

title: Gardens of Adn, their doors already open for them.
subtitle: A welcome, not a locked gate
then: Ibn Kathir explains Adn as {reward}eternal gardens{/reward}. The doors will be opened for them, meaning {reward}when they come, the gates open for them{/reward}. This was promised to believers who were being mocked and pressured in Makkah.
now: You know the feeling: the office with the keycard that will not work, the visa office queue, the door you have to talk your way through. {reward}Here the doors open for you as you arrive.{/reward}
old: Paradise feels distant, like a place I would have to beg to enter.
new: For those who hold to taqwa, the doors are opened in welcome.
try: Make a short dua today asking Allah to open the doors of Paradise for you and your family.

title: Reclining, they call for fruit and drink in abundance.
subtitle: Rest after a life of effort
then: Ibn Kathir says they will recline, and {reward}whatever they ask for, they will find it{/reward}, prepared just as they wanted. Whatever drink they want will be brought to them. The image is one of complete ease.
now: Night shift, school run, the dishes again. Your body aches and there is no break in sight. {reward}A day is coming where you simply sit, ask, and receive.{/reward} The tiredness here is not the end of the story.
old: I will finally rest once life here gets easier.
new: The true rest is ahead, and today's effort for Allah is building toward it.
try: Offer today's most tiring task to Allah with a quiet intention before you start it.

title: Beside them, faithful companions of equal age.
subtitle: Companionship without betrayal
then: Ibn Kathir explains these companions as those who {reward}restrain their glances from anyone except their husbands{/reward}, and do not turn to anyone else. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and others said of equal ages means they will all be the same age.
now: Trust is fragile here: messages you should not have seen, a friend who drifted, a home where loyalty was broken. {reward}In Paradise, companionship is faithful.{/reward} Begin practising that loyalty now.
old: Loyalty is rare, and people always drift eventually.
new: Paradise holds companionship with complete faithfulness, and I can practise it now.
try: Guard your eyes and phone today for the sake of the person you love.

title: This is what you are promised for the Day of Account.
subtitle: The same Day they mocked is the Day you hope for
then: Earlier the deniers mockingly asked for their share before the Day of Account. Now Allah says to the righteous: {reward}this is what you are promised for the Day of Account{/reward}. Ibn Kathir says it is for those resurrected from their graves and {idea}saved from the Fire{/idea}.
now: When you think of the Day of Judgement, maybe you only feel fear. {reward}For those who try, it is also the day a promise is kept.{/reward} Fear and hope together.
old: The Day of Account is only something to dread.
new: It is also the Day Allah keeps His promise to those who held to taqwa.
try: When you think of the Hereafter today, pair one fear with one hope.

title: Our provision, which never runs out.
subtitle: What lasts versus what drains away
then: Allah says Paradise {reward}will never come to an end or disappear{/reward}. Ibn Kathir links it to the verse that {trap}whatever is with you will be exhausted{/trap}, and whatever is with Allah will remain, and to a gift without end.
now: Payday, then two weeks later the account is thin again. The holiday ends. The new phone gets old. {reward}Nothing here is built to last. What Allah provides there does not run out.{/reward}
old: Security means building up enough here so it does not run out.
new: Everything here runs out. Only what is with Allah never ends.
try: Move a small amount from what runs out into charity, which lasts with Allah.

title: That is one end. The transgressors have an evil return.
subtitle: Two destinations placed side by side
then: Having described the end of the blessed, Allah mentions {trap}the end of the doomed{/trap}. Ibn Kathir says the taghin are those who disobey Allah and oppose His Messengers. Their return is the worst return.
now: You just read about open gates and lasting provision, and you felt hopeful. {idea}The surah does not let you skip the other side.{/idea} Both are told so you choose your direction while you can.
old: Talk of punishment is for other, much worse people.
new: Both ends are shown to me so I can choose my direction honestly.
try: Ask yourself one honest question today: which way did my choices point this week?

title: Hell, which they enter, and a wretched place to rest.
subtitle: The opposite of the reclining in Paradise
then: Ibn Kathir says they will enter Hell and {trap}it will overwhelm them on all sides{/trap}. Allah calls it the worst place to rest, set against the reclining ease of the righteous described just before.
now: You chase comfort: the easy shortcut, the lie that saves you a hard conversation. {idea}Some comforts now lead to the worst rest later.{/idea} The harder honest path leads to real ease.
old: Whatever makes life easier right now is good for me.
new: Comfort bought with disobedience leads to the worst resting place.
try: Choose the honest option once today, even if it is the less comfortable one.

title: Extreme heat and extreme cold: let them taste it.
subtitle: The opposite of the drinks in Paradise
then: Ibn Kathir explains {trap}hamim as something heated to the ultimate degree{/trap}, and ghassaq as its opposite, something so cold it is unbearable. It mirrors the drinks brought to the righteous in the verses before.
now: You know how one choice can leave a taste for days: a harsh word, a broken promise. {idea}Deeds have a taste, here and there.{/idea} The good news is that you still choose what you will taste.
old: What I do today has no flavour that follows me.
new: Every deed has a taste that returns to me, so I choose deeds I would want to taste.
try: Do one kind thing today whose taste you would be happy to meet again.

title: And other punishments of the same kind, in pairs.
subtitle: Opposites that bring no relief
then: Ibn Kathir says this means other things of this kind, {trap}a thing and its opposite{/trap}, serving as punishments. Al-Hasan Al-Basri said different kinds of punishments. Others mentioned intense cold and heat as paired opposites.
now: You try to fix one bad habit by swapping it for another: from overspending to overworking, from anger to cold silence. {idea}Swinging to the opposite extreme is not the same as being healed.{/idea} Turning to Allah is.
old: If one extreme is bad, the opposite extreme must be fine.
new: Real relief is not in swinging between extremes but in turning back to Allah.
try: Notice one area where you swing between extremes. Pick a balanced middle step for today.

title: Here comes another crowd with you. No welcome for them.
subtitle: Those who walked together turn on each other
then: Ibn Kathir says this describes what the people of Hell say to one another. Instead of greeting, {trap}they curse one another and reject one another{/trap}. When a new group arrives, it is said: here is a troop entering with you, no welcome for them.
now: The friends who egg you on to skip class, the group that laughs at things you know are wrong. {trap}Bonds built on wrongdoing do not hold.{/trap} {idea}Choose friends you would be glad to meet on that Day.{/idea}
old: Friends who join me in wrong are still true friends.
new: Companionship built on disobedience turns into blame in the end.
try: Send a warm message to one friend who helps you be better.

title: No welcome for you! You brought this on us.
subtitle: Followers blame those who led them
then: The incoming group answers back: {trap}no welcome for you either{/trap}. Ibn Kathir explains their words as: you called us to that which led us to this fate. Both groups end up in the same evil place to stay.
now: Your friend said the shortcut was fine, the influencer said it was halal, the colleague said everyone does it. {idea}Following someone does not move the responsibility off your shoulders.{/idea}
old: If someone else talked me into it, it is on them, not me.
new: I answer for whom I chose to follow.
try: Before acting on advice today, ask yourself whether you would still do it if no one had suggested it.

title: Our Lord, double the punishment of whoever led us here.
subtitle: Blaming others brings no relief
then: They ask Allah to {trap}double the torment{/trap} of whoever brought this on them. Ibn Kathir links it to the verse where Allah answers that each has a double, {idea}each punished as he deserves{/idea}. Blaming the other does not reduce one's own account.
now: Something goes wrong at home and the whole family argument becomes: whose fault was it more? {idea}Even if they were more to blame, your part is still yours.{/idea} Owning it is where repair starts.
old: If someone else is more to blame, my part does not really count.
new: Their larger share does not erase my own, so I deal with mine.
try: In your next argument, name your own part first, before theirs.

title: Where are the men we used to call the worst?
subtitle: The people they looked down on are missing
then: Ibn Kathir says the disbelievers will notice that {trap}the people they thought misguided{/trap} are not with them. Mujahid said Abu Jahl will say: why do I not see Bilal, Ammar and Suhayb? They will find that those believers are {reward}in the lofty levels of Paradise{/reward}.
now: The cleaner at your office, the quiet neighbour with the old car, the relative everyone jokes about. {idea}You may be looking down on someone Allah has raised.{/idea}
old: I can tell who the worthless people are by how they look and live.
new: Those I look down on may be the ones Allah has honored most.
try: Greet warmly today someone you usually overlook, and mean it.

title: Did we only mock them, or are our eyes missing them?
subtitle: Wishful thinking at the very end
then: They ask whether they {trap}took those believers as an object of mockery{/trap} in the world, or whether their eyes have simply failed to find them. Ibn Kathir says they console themselves with {trap}wishful thinking{/trap}, then learn the believers are in Paradise.
now: The group chat that turns one person into a running joke. The nickname that stuck. {trap}Mocking someone blinds you to who they really are.{/trap} The joke can be the thing that hides the truth.
old: Mocking people a bit is just harmless fun.
new: Ridicule can blind me to the worth Allah sees in someone.
try: If a joke about someone starts today, change the subject or say something good about them.

title: That quarrel of the people of the Fire is true.
subtitle: A real scene told in advance
then: Ibn Kathir says Allah tells the Prophet ﷺ that {idea}this account of the dispute and cursing among the people of Hell is true{/idea}, with no doubt in it. It was told in Makkah, to people still able to change.
now: You have read the whole scene: the blaming, the cursing, the empty search. {idea}You are not in it. You are reading it in advance{/idea}, on an ordinary day, with time to choose differently.
old: Descriptions of the Hereafter are distant and not about my choices.
new: It is told to me in advance so I can live differently now.
try: Make peace with one person today you have been quarrelling with.

title: Only a warner, and no god but Allah, the One.
subtitle: The Prophet ﷺ states plainly who he is
then: Allah tells the Prophet ﷺ to say to those who denied him: {idea}I am a warner, I am not as you claim{/idea}. This answers the labels from the start of the surah. Ibn Kathir explains the Irresistible as the One who {idea}alone has subjugated and controlled everything{/idea}.
now: People online have a label ready for you: too religious, not religious enough, old fashioned. {idea}You do not have to argue with every label.{/idea} Say plainly what you are, and point to Allah.
old: I have to defend myself against every label people give me.
new: I can say simply who I am and leave the rest to Allah, the One.
try: Next time you are mislabeled, answer in one calm sentence and move on.

title: Lord of the heavens and earth, the Mighty, the Ever-Forgiving.
subtitle: Power and forgiveness in the same breath
then: Ibn Kathir says Allah is {idea}the Sovereign of all that and in control of it{/idea}. He is {reward}Oft-Forgiving as well as being Almighty{/reward}. The warning of the Prophet ﷺ comes with an open door.
now: Your boss has power and uses it to punish mistakes. Maybe you are like that with your kids. {reward}Allah's might sits right next to His forgiveness.{/reward} The One who could crush you keeps forgiving you.
old: Someone that powerful must be harsh with my mistakes.
new: The Almighty is also the Ever-Forgiving, so I come back to Him without fear of a closed door.
try: Say Ya Ghaffar, forgive me, three times today, thinking of one specific mistake.

title: Say: it is great news.
subtitle: The message is the biggest headline there is
then: Ibn Kathir says the great news is {idea}something very important{/idea}: that Allah has sent His Messenger ﷺ to them. In a city arguing over gods and status, this was the headline that mattered most.
now: Breaking news alerts all day: politics, prices, celebrity drama. Your phone buzzes and you check every time. {idea}The greatest news has already been delivered.{/idea} It does not buzz. You have to open it.
old: The Quran is old news. What is happening today matters more.
new: The message is the greatest news I will ever receive.
try: Before checking the news today, read one verse with its meaning first.

title: Great news, and you turn away from it.
subtitle: Neglect is a quieter kind of rejection
then: Ibn Kathir explains turning away simply: {trap}you neglect it{/trap}. The chiefs rejected loudly, but neglect is the wider problem. The greatest news can be ignored without anyone saying a word against it.
now: The Quran on the shelf, dusted at Eid. The app installed, opened in Ramadan. {trap}You never rejected it. You just never got to it.{/trap} Neglect is quiet, and it adds up.
old: As long as I do not reject the Quran, I am fine.
new: Leaving it unopened is also a way of turning away.
try: Put a Quran or the app somewhere you will see it first thing tomorrow, and open it once.

title: I had no knowledge of the assembly on high.
subtitle: The story he could only know by revelation
then: Ibn Kathir says it means: {idea}were it not for revelation, how could I have known{/idea} about the dispute on high? It refers to the matter of Adam, and how Iblis refused to prostrate and argued with his Lord. The story follows next.
now: Your friend asks a question about the unseen and you feel you have to have an answer. {idea}Even the Prophet ﷺ said: I only know what was revealed.{/idea} It is fine to say Allah knows best.
old: I should have an answer for everything about religion.
new: What we know of the unseen comes only from revelation, and the rest I leave to Allah.
try: When asked something you do not know about the deen today, say: I am not sure, Allah knows best.

title: All that is revealed to me: I am a clear warner.
subtitle: Clear about his role, nothing added
then: The passage ends with the Prophet ﷺ saying that what is revealed to him is only that {idea}he is a plain warner{/idea}. Ibn Kathir's heading for this section: the message of the Messenger ﷺ is great news.
now: You have tried for years to get your brother back to prayer. You feel like a failure. {idea}Your job is to say it clearly and kindly.{/idea} Guidance is not in your hands.
old: If someone I care about does not change, I have failed.
new: My part is to remind clearly and kindly. Guidance belongs to Allah.
try: Make dua for one person you have been trying to remind, and let go of the pressure.

title: Your Lord told the angels: I will create a human from clay.
subtitle: The start of the story behind the dispute
then: Ibn Kathir notes this story appears in Al-Baqarah, Al-Araf, Al-Hijr, Al-Isra, Al-Kahf and here. {idea}Before creating Adam, Allah told the angels{/idea} He would create a human being from clay. The plain material was about to be honored.
now: You feel ordinary: average job, average looks, nothing special. {idea}Humanity began as clay, and Allah announced it to the angels.{/idea} What you are made of does not limit what Allah can honor.
old: I am too ordinary to matter much.
new: Allah made humans from clay and still announced them with honor.
try: Thank Allah today for one ordinary thing about yourself that you usually ignore.

title: When I have shaped him and breathed in the soul, bow down.
subtitle: Honor came with the soul from Allah
then: Ibn Kathir says the angels were told to prostrate to Adam {reward}as a sign of honor and respect{/reward}, and {idea}out of obedience to the command of Allah{/idea}. It was not worship of Adam. It was obedience to the One who commanded it.
now: You scroll past people all day as if they were furniture: the delivery driver, the cashier, the person in the ward bed. {idea}Each one is a child of Adam, whom Allah honored.{/idea}
old: Most people I pass are just background.
new: Every human is a child of Adam, whom Allah honored, and deserves respect.
try: Look the next service worker you meet in the eye, smile, and thank them by name if you can.

title: The angels prostrated, all of them together.
subtitle: Obedience without argument
then: Ibn Kathir says {reward}all of the angels obeyed this command{/reward}. The verse stresses all of them, every one. No angel asked why a creature of clay should be honored. They obeyed their Lord.
now: You know Fajr is due and the alarm is ringing. Part of you wants a reason, a debate, five more minutes. {reward}The angels simply bowed.{/reward} Sometimes obedience is the answer to the debate.
old: I will obey once I fully understand every reason.
new: Trusting Allah means I can obey before I see every reason.
try: Do one act of worship today right when it is due, without bargaining with yourself.

title: Except Iblis: he was arrogant and became a disbeliever.
subtitle: One refusal, and its root
then: Ibn Kathir says Iblis {trap}was not one of the angels; he was one of the jinn{/trap}, and his nature betrayed him at his time of greatest need. He refused, disputed with his Lord, and so {trap}committed the sin of disbelief{/trap}. Arrogance came first.
now: Your parent asks you to apologise to your younger sibling. You know you were wrong. {trap}But bowing to them feels beneath you.{/trap} That feeling is the same seed.
old: My refusals are reasonable. I just have my standards.
new: The first refusal in history came from arrogance, so I watch for it in my own no.
try: Apologise today to someone you consider beneath you, for one specific thing.

title: What stopped you from bowing to the one I honored?
subtitle: Allah asks Iblis to name his reason
then: Allah asks Iblis what prevented him from prostrating to {idea}the one He created with His hands{/idea}. Was it pride, or did he see himself among the exalted? Ibn Kathir says Iblis {trap}disputed with his Lord{/trap} instead of returning.
now: Your conscience asks you directly: why did you not help when you could have? {idea}That question is a door.{/idea} You can walk through it with honesty, or slam it with an excuse.
old: When I am questioned, I need to defend myself.
new: When my conscience asks why, it is an invitation to come back, not to argue.
try: Next time you feel the urge to defend yourself today, pause and ask if they might be right.

title: I am better than him: fire versus clay.
subtitle: The oldest argument of pride
then: Iblis claimed he was better because {trap}he was created from fire and Adam from clay, and fire was better than clay, or so he said{/trap}. Ibn Kathir says he made a mistake and went against Allah's command. Allah then cast him out of His mercy.
now: Better family, better school, better postcode, better passport. {trap}I am better than him{/trap} still gets said, just in new words. {idea}Allah never asked what you were made of. He asked whether you obeyed.{/idea}
old: Where I come from makes me better than some people.
new: Worth is not in my origin but in my obedience to Allah.
try: Catch one thought today that starts with I am better than, and replace it with a dua for that person.

title: Get out from here, for you are cast out.
subtitle: Pride cost Iblis his place
then: Ibn Kathir says Allah {trap}exiled him, humiliated him, and cast him out of His mercy and His sacred presence{/trap}. He cast him down from the heavens to the earth, disgraced. The one who claimed to be higher ended up lowest.
now: The person who insists on being the most important in every room usually ends up left out of the room. {trap}Pride promises height and delivers a fall.{/trap} {idea}Humility is the safer ground.{/idea}
old: Holding my head high above others keeps my place secure.
new: Pride is what costs a place. Humility keeps it.
try: Let someone else take the credit or the front seat once today, gladly.

title: My curse is on you until the Day of Recompense.
subtitle: Despair of mercy, by his own choice
then: Ibn Kathir says Allah called him Iblis, {trap}symbolizing that he had despaired of mercy{/trap}, that there was no hope for him of mercy. The curse stands until the Day of Recompense. He argued instead of returning.
now: You made the same mistake again. A voice says: you are too far gone, why bother. {idea}That voice wants you to despair, like he did.{/idea} Do not take his name. Turn back.
old: I have gone too far for Allah's mercy now.
new: Despair of mercy is Iblis's way. A believer keeps returning.
try: Whatever you feel too far gone about, make one sincere istighfar for it today.

title: My Lord, give me respite until they are raised.
subtitle: He asked for time, not forgiveness
then: Ibn Kathir says Iblis {trap}asked Allah to give him a reprieve until the Day of Resurrection{/trap}. Cast out of mercy, the one thing he did not ask for was forgiveness. He wanted time, and he had already decided what to use it for.
now: You ask Allah for a longer life, a better job, more time before the deadline. {idea}How often do you also ask: forgive me?{/idea} Time without returning to Him is not the gift it seems.
old: What I need most from Allah is more time.
new: Time is only a gift if I use it to come back to Him.
try: In your next dua, ask for forgiveness before you ask for anything else.

title: You are among those given respite.
subtitle: The Forbearing does not hasten to punish
then: Ibn Kathir says {idea}the Forbearing One, who does not hasten to punish those who disobey Him{/idea}, gave him a reprieve. Being given time did not mean being approved of. It meant the test went on.
now: You did something wrong and nothing happened. No consequence, no one found out. {idea}Allah's patience with you is not approval.{/idea} It is room to turn around.
old: If nothing bad happened, it must not have been that wrong.
new: Allah's patience gives me time to return, not permission to continue.
try: Think of one wrong that seemed to have no consequence, and fix what you can of it today.

title: Until the Day of the appointed time.
subtitle: Even the respite has an end
then: Allah grants the respite only {idea}until the Day of the time appointed{/idea}. Ibn Kathir notes that once Iblis knew he was safe from destruction until then, {trap}he rebelled and transgressed{/trap}. Feeling safe made him bolder.
now: When you feel there is plenty of time, you get careless: the prayer can wait, the apology can wait. {trap}Feeling safe made Iblis bolder.{/trap} {idea}Every respite has a date.{/idea}
old: I have years ahead, so there is no rush to change.
new: Every respite ends at a set time, so feeling safe should not make me careless.
try: Do one thing today you keep postponing because you think you have time.

title: By Your might, I will mislead them all.
subtitle: The enemy announced his plan
then: Once safe until the Day, Iblis swore {trap}I will surely mislead them all{/trap}. Ibn Kathir links it to another verse where he says he will seize and mislead Adam's offspring, all but a few. His goal is stated openly.
now: The late night scroll that turns into something you regret. The thought that you deserve it just this once. {trap}It is not random.{/trap} {idea}Knowing there is a plan against you is half the defense.{/idea}
old: My slips just happen. There is nothing behind them.
new: Shaytan openly vowed to mislead me, so I guard myself on purpose.
try: Say A'udhu billahi min ash-shaytan ir-rajim the next time a bad urge starts today.

title: Except Your sincere servants among them.
subtitle: The ones he admits he cannot reach
then: Iblis himself excepts {reward}Your true servants{/reward}. Ibn Kathir connects them to the verse where Allah says: {reward}My servants, you have no authority over them{/reward}, and your Lord is enough as a Guardian.
now: You have tried fighting the habit with willpower and apps and timers. {reward}The verse points to something deeper: sincerity.{/reward} Doing it for Allah alone is the place he cannot reach.
old: Resisting temptation depends on how strong I am.
new: Sincere servants of Allah are the ones he has no power over.
try: Before one good deed today, pause and make the intention for Allah alone.

title: The truth, and the truth is what I say.
subtitle: Allah's reply to Iblis's oath
then: Mujahid read it as {idea}I am the Truth, and the truth I say{/idea}. Another report from him: the truth is from Me and I speak the truth. As-Suddi saw it as an oath sworn by Allah. It answers the oath Iblis had just made.
now: Loud voices tell you who you are and where you are going: ads, critics, your own worst thoughts. {idea}Only One speaks nothing but truth.{/idea} Let His word be the one you trust most.
old: The loudest voices around me tell the truth about my life.
new: Allah is the Truth and speaks only truth. His word outlasts every other.
try: Replace one negative thing you tell yourself with a verse that says otherwise.

title: I will fill Hell with you and those who follow you.
subtitle: Following him is a choice with an end
then: Allah says He will fill Hell with Iblis {trap}and those who follow him{/trap}, together. Ibn Kathir links it to the verse: go, and whoever of them follows you, Hell will be the recompense of you all. {idea}Following is the key word.{/idea}
now: You hear the whisper, but you are the one who picks up the phone, opens the tab, says the cruel thing. {idea}He invites. You decide.{/idea} That means you can also decide not to.
old: Shaytan made me do it.
new: He can only call. Following him is my choice, and so is refusing.
try: Notice one moment today when you could follow an urge, and choose not to.

title: I ask no payment, and I do not pretend.
subtitle: A message offered freely, without additions
then: Ibn Kathir says the Prophet ﷺ asked {idea}no reward from the goods of this world{/idea}, and did not add anything to what Allah told him. Ibn Masud cited this verse and said: whoever knows should say it, and whoever does not should say {idea}Allah knows best{/idea}.
now: Someone in the family chat asks a religious question and you feel the pressure to sound knowledgeable. {idea}Saying I do not know is part of knowledge.{/idea} No need to dress up a guess.
old: Admitting I do not know makes me look ignorant.
new: Saying Allah knows best when I do not know is part of real knowledge.
try: Help someone today without expecting anything back, not even thanks.

title: It is only a reminder for all the worlds.
subtitle: The surah opened with a reminder and closes with one
then: Ibn Abbas said the Quran is {idea}a reminder for all who are held accountable, humans and jinn{/idea}. Ibn Kathir links it to the verse: that I may warn you and whomever it reaches. The surah began with an oath by the Quran full of reminding, and ends here.
now: You have read this surah on your phone, in a language far from Makkah, centuries later. {idea}It reached you. That makes it yours.{/idea}
old: This was addressed to people long ago.
new: It is a reminder for everyone it reaches, and it has reached me.
try: Share one verse from this surah with someone, with its meaning, today.

title: And you will surely know its truth after a while.
subtitle: Every person will see it confirmed
then: Ibn Kathir says it means {idea}you will see confirmation that what he says is true{/idea}, and soon. Qatadah said after death. Ikrimah said on the Day of Resurrection. There is no contradiction, because whoever dies enters the matters of that Day.
now: Everyone will know eventually. The question is only when you know it: now, while it can shape your mornings and your choices, or later, when it simply confirms. {idea}Knowing now is the mercy.{/idea}
old: I will be certain about all this when I see it for myself.
new: Everyone will see it is true in the end, so I let it change me now.
try: Choose one change this surah asked of you, and start it today.
